messages.subject: exposing stan functions to R requires at least two parameters???
parts:
I am getting an odd error when trying to expose a Stan function to R.  The function works if I have two input parameters in the Stan function, the second being a dummy, but returns an error if only one parameter is required.  The following R code with "mc" works, but "mc2" returns an error "In Rcpp::sourceCpp(code = paste(lines, collapse = "\n")) :
  No Rcpp::export attributes or RCPP_MODULE declarations found in source"

The only difference appears to be that the first function has two inputs, the second has one. (There also seems to be a bug when you write a function with no input parameters)

mc <- '
functions {
    vector fib(int n, real x) {
      vector[n] fib;
      fib[1] <- 1;
      fib[2] <- 1;
      for (i in 3:n) {
        fib[i] <- fib[i-1] + fib[i-2];
      }
      return fib;
    }
}

model {

}  
'

mc2 <- 
  '
functions {
    vector fib2(int n) {
      vector[n] fib2;
      fib2[1] <- 1;
      fib2[2] <- 1;
      for (i in 3:n) {
        fib2[i] <- fib2[i-1] + fib2[i-2];
      }
      return fib2;
    }
}

model {

}  
'
cppcode <- stanc(model_code = mc, model_name = "Demonstration2")
expose_stan_functions(cppcode)
fib(200, x=1)

cppcode2 <- stanc(model_code = mc2, model_name = "Demonstration3")
expose_stan_functions(cppcode2)
fib2(200)

messages.subject: Complex hierarchical model --- any hints?
parts:
Dear all,

I'm still having trouble with non-efficient sampling in my hierarchical
model (I already tried some things, see earlier e-mails). Intriguingly,
often all four chains behave nicely except one. Or suddenly, out of
nowhere, a chain get trapped for a long period.

I prepared a simplified* version of this model and attached it. Maybe
someone can have a quick look if there are some obvious mistakes. We
haven't been working with Bayesian statistics for too long and
especially I switched only recently to Stan (in the hope HMC can better
deal with this model).

The general structure of the model is as follows (in bottom-up order):
- on the stimulus level layer: positive outcomes are binomially
distributed at each level
- on the subject layer: a custom psychometric function describes the
success rates at different levels
- on the group layer: parameters of the mentioned function are drawn
from normal group distributions

Many thanks and best regards
Jan

* I made the following simplifications:
- deleted model structure of a second identical condition
- deleted a huge generated quantities block, mostly containing
differences between the two conditions
- included dummy data within the script. Only 10 data sets are
included, whereas the model is intended to run on 20+ data sets
eventually. With half the data it is even more stubborn ...

P.S.: I jut obtained a 3000 iterations test sample with the file that
doesn't look too bad. However, I've seen this before and faced the
mention problems then after 20000 iterations or so ...

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Complex hierarchical model --- any hints?
parts:
Hi, here are some quick thoughts:
1. We recommend putting the Stan program in a separate .stan file rather than encoding it as a character string. That’ll be easier when you want to fit the model more than once.

2. Hard constraints on parameters are typically a good idea. Inherent constraints (such as sigma>0) are fine, but constraints such as <-.2,.2> are typically a badd idea. Better to use a prior, for example replacing a hard <-.2,.2> constraint by a prior such as N(0,.1) or N(0,.2).
3. Similarly for the parameter you bound between 0.01 and 0.99. If it can’t be 0.995, it probably is highly unlikely to be 0.985. Etc.
4. No need to write 0 and 8 as 0.0 and 8.0.
5. The Cauchy priors could be a bit weak. I suggest replacing by normal or something like t_3 or t_7 if you want some long tails.
I suspect that none of these tips will solve your problem, but who knows? Maybe! I’m thinking it can’t hurt to put in some priors.
A

The cauchy's just a weakly informative prior --- if you have more info
about your distribution's tails, by all means use it!

The only place integers should matter in Stan is (1.0 / 3.0) vs. (1 / 3).

Chains typically get stuck in hierarchical models with wildly varying posterior
scales. You can try reducing initial step size and increasing the
target acceptance rate, which will slow down the model but make it more
robust to getting stuck.

parts:
Yes, fitting other models counts. It doesn't match the
prescriptive theory of Bayes (choose a prior, observe some
data, update to posterior), but it matches the practice of
model criticism and updating.

If you have one parameter in (0,1) and another in (0,100)
range, you probably want to bring them both down into the (-1/2, 1/2)
range or (-1,1) scale. (Not a hard constraint, just most of
the probability mass.) But that'd require multiplying and
shifting.

The way to control those parameters varies in name by interface,
but the doc of what they do is in the Stan language manual in the
part on algorithms.

- Bob

The problem is that those non-converging chains may be indicating
that there's something biased in the sample you do get. When they
get stuck, it's usually because the sampler fell into a tightly
constrained neck of a funnel somewhere --- if you don't explore
the necks of the funnels, you get biased estimates. But if you
try to explore them with too-large step sizes, the sampler virtually
hangs, never being able to find the escape direction.

- Bob

parts:
RStan's set up to parallelize by default as of 2.8.0.

I believe 1 or 0.1 is the default, so 0.01 is a small-ish initial
step size. It's all problem dependent. We set things up assuming
all parameters were roughly normal(0, 1) distributed.

You can also look at where you're having problems in ShinyStan
(or even in some of the RStan output, I believe). If you're getting
stuck way out in the tail, then you might be able to initialize in
a more reasonable place and avoid the problem. But if you're getting
stuck in a volume of high posterior mass, then you might need
to reparameterize into a more favorable posterior geometry.

- Bob

“Noninformative” and “conservative” are loaded terms with little formal
meaning, so you’re probably not going to get a particularly satisfactory
answer.  When you model you have to make assumptions, whether
it be in the form of the likelihood and the prior (the hierarchical structure)
or the hyperpriors.  The best you can really judge is whether or not those
assumptions are qualitatively consistent with the given data which requires
doing posterior predictive checks.

Andrew is just saying that O(10) is probably still extreme if you have
standardized all of your data so that your random effects should be O(1).
Tightening the prior will improve your posterior inferences provided that
you don’t tighten it so far that you start introducing tension with the data.

On Thursday, November 5, 2015 at 7:23:17 PM UTC-5, Krzysztof Sakrejda wrote:
It would have been nice if all Stan distributions went either with scale or rate parameterization but....

Well, we mostly went with BDA parameterizations which often followed Bayesian conventions and Bayesian conventions were usually designed to facilitate Gibbs sampling. And as we went along, we came to realize how important it is to establish a reasonable scale for parameters when using the default sampler in Stan. So, it probably would have been better to use scale parameterizations from the outset. But for priors on unknown quantities, it is typically a good idea to define a primitive in the parameters block whose prior entails scale = 1 = rate and than multiply that primitive by your prior scale inside the transformed parameters block to get the quantity that corresponds to the algebraic representation of the log-likelihood.

Ben

parts:
On Thursday, November 5, 2015 at 10:45:39 PM UTC-5, Andrew Gelman wrote:
I don’t know, it’s just the way they always wrote it in the textbooks.  When I learned probability theory in 1981, my textbook had the exponential distribution and it was parameterized according to the rate parameter.  Nothing Bayesian about it, it’s just the convention.

I would agree that the frequentists had conventions about parameterizations prior to Gibbs sampling but, at least for maximum likelihood, the frequentists didn't have a frequentist justification for one parameterization over another due to the invariance property. Substantively, in the context of a duration model, it could either make sense to think of events occurring at some rate or to think about the mean of an exponential process.

But I don't think substantive reasons should be that relevant to how Stan parameterizes distributions because a user could just declare a rate parameter in the parameters block, specify an informative prior on the rate in the model block, and flip it over when putting into a likelihood that is parameterized in terms of scale (or vice versa). For technical reasons, it seems that HMC is more suited to scale (re)parameterizations, but those parameterizations tend to run counter to the parameterizations Bayesians were using for technical reasons when they were developing Gibbs samplers.

Ben
